Question: What are the benefits of studying rocks and minerals in school?
Answer: In my UK high school the choice in years 11 and 12 was between German or Geology - so it was a bit of a no-brainer. Geology was my favourite subject in those two years - and I loved the field trips. It led to me studying Mining Engineering at University and a lifelong career in the mining industry. The best parts of my career were when I interacted with the exploration geologists to figure out whether what they had found could be turned into an economically feasible mine. Among other projects, I reviewed the La Plata coal mine project in New Mexico, and later became the mine manager there. I also worked on the feasibility of the Escondida copper mine in the Atacama desert in Chile, which has now become the world’s largest copper mine. Some projects never made it, but still held lots of interest. I well remember visiting a gallium and germanium project in Utah, and the huge, but flawed diamond we found in a kimberlite pipe in South Africa. I met lots of interesting people along the way. I especially remember Hugo Dummet, whose theories about where and how glaciers in Canada had transported minerals across the continent led to the discovery of the Ekati diamond mine.

Question: Why is there no consensus on the age of Earth?
Answer: There is consensus on the age of the Earth. Actually, there is not one but two consensuses. Scientists who study the subject generally agree that the formation of the Earth occurred 4.54 billion years ago, with an uncertainty of about 50 million years - i.e. the age of the Earth has been determined with a possible error of a little over 1%. The age was determined from radiometric dating of meteorites, which are judged to be representative of the material that formed the Earth. This age is consistent with ages determined from rocks on Earth - notably Archaean lead ores of galena. I don’t know of any recognized scientist disputing this age on scientific principles. On the other hand, Creationists, who believe in a literal interpretation of the Bible, put the age of the Earth at about 6000 years. Most famously Archbishop Ussher estimated that the Earth was formed at midday on October 22nd 4004 BC, based on the ages of the Patriarchs listed in the Bible and other evidence from Middle Eastern kings. As to why the two groups cannot agree, I would refer you to the famous line from the Reverend Sydney Smith who observed two woman arguing across a street from windows in the upper floors of their houses. Smith said “those women will never agree because they are arguing from different premises.”

Question: Is it true that before the Earth was fully completed, with an orbiting Moon, Venus had several billion years in our younger smaller Sun's Goldilocks Zone?
Answer: Yes it is quite likely that Venus was much more Earth-like in the early years of the solar system. As noted the early sun was fainter than at present and emitted only about 70% of the energy that it does now. This fainter sun would have placed Venus squarely in the Goldilocks zone with liquid water and possibly oceans. Question: How are oxygen isotope records of marine sediments used to understand glacial-interglacial cycles?
Answer: Oxygen has three stable isotopes. Oxygen 16, whose nucleus contains 8 protons, and 8 neutrons makes up 99.76% of the oxygen in the atmosphere. Oxygen 17, with 8 protons, and nine neutrons makes up 0.04%, and oxygen 18 with 8 protons and 10 neutrons makes up 0.2%. Oxygen isotope analysis usually measures the ratio of oxygen 18 to oxygen 16. Because water containing Oxygen 18 is 11% heavier than water with Oxygen 16 and because the extra neutrons affect the hydrogen bonds, water with Oxygen 18 requires more energy to vaporize and releases more energy when it condenses and diffuses less readily than water with Oxygen 16. Note that heavy water with two atoms of deuterium has similar properties to water with Oxygen 18, but deuterium makes up only 0.01% of hydrogen and water with two atoms of deuterium is very rare. In the global circulation water tends to be evaporated from the oceans in the warmer lower latitudes and precipitates out as rain as winds move it towards the poles. Because the water containing Oxygen 18 is harder to evaporate and easier to precipitate, precipitation at higher latitudes is depleted in Oxygen 18. During glacial periods this depleted water may be locked up in glacial ice and does not return to the ocean. In consequence the water in the oceans becomes enriched in Oxygen 18. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the water reacts with water molecules to form carbonic acid (H2CO3), which ionizes to two hydrogen ions and a carbonate ion (CO3 - -). If the water molecule contains Oxygen 18, the carbonate ion will contain two atoms of Oxygen 16 and one atom of Oxygen 18. Shelly creatures react calcium ions in the water with the carbonate ions to form calcium carbonate (CaCO3), which they use to build their shells. Shells which are formed during glacial periods will thus be very slightly enriched with Oxygen 18, compared to Oxygen 16. The shells of choice used for analysis are the abundant tiny foraminifera. The ratio of Oxygen 18 to Oxygen 16 can be accurately determined with a mass spectrometer. The above is a simplified explanation. The paper at gives a much more thorough explanation. The chart below (and the image of foraminifera above) are taken from this paper. Because natural fractionations are, in practice, quite small, and Oxygen 18 is always very much rarer than Oxygen 16, the isotopic ratios of natural materials are generally quite close to the average value. Small differences between small numbers are un-wieldy, so (as is the convention for other stable isotope systems) oxygen isotope ratios are generally quoted as deviations (delta values) from the oxygen isotope ratio (δ18O) of a standard sub-stance in parts per thousand ('per mil', signified by the symbol, ‘‰’). There are good, practical reasons for this convention because isotope ratios of sample materials are almost always measured relative to a laboratory standard rather than as an absolute ratio, which is much more difficult to determine accurately. Note that if a sample has a positive δ18O, it is said to be enriched in the heavy isotope relative to the standard and, if negative, it is said to be depleted. It so happens that two different standard values are in widespread use from which these delta-values are quoted: Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW) and Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB, which is a carbonate standard.
